% predictions: results/ext/PREREG.md. Both graph miners (macros with suffixes Gpt and Oss).

\subsection{External Checks}
\label{sec:exp-external}

LoCoBench is synthetic, its edits are explicit, and its gold follows our committee's reading. We
therefore tested the paper's claims on five datasets that others built and labelled, and on
shuffled LoCoBench texts, with every prediction, test and threshold pre-registered before any graph
of these checks was mined (App.~\ref{app:external}); analyses outside the pre-registration are
marked \emph{exploratory}. The claims tested are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item that the score measures logical rather than discourse coherence;
\item that it falls when a natural text contradicts itself;
\item that a relation's sign follows the truth values;
\item that the miner and the compile map agree with independent human annotation.
\end{itemize}
Claims are sentences, except in LoCoBench, which keeps its own claims, in QT30, where they are the
corpus's propositions, and in GDTB, where they are the two arguments of a relation. Relations come from the graph-level miner of
\S\ref{sec:mining} with the two models of \S\ref{sec:exp-mined}, GPT-6 and gpt-oss-120b (two arms, named by their
model), and $\LCS$ uses flat priors. The text reports
GPT-6 and notes where gpt-oss-120b differs. Table~\ref{tab:external} gives each
pre-registered hypothesis with its result, and Figure~\ref{fig:external} summarizes three of
them.

\paragraph{Logical, not discourse, coherence.} Three results separate the score from discourse
coherence.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{It is unrelated to rated coherence.} On SummEval's \extSeN{} summaries, $\LCS$ is
  uncorrelated with the experts' coherence ratings ($\rho=\extSeRhoCohGpt$), as predicted.
\item \textbf{With GPT-6, order does not move it beyond sampling noise.} The pre-registered comparison under
  permutation failed, but Figure~\ref{fig:external}a shows why. On LoCoBench, $\LCS$ stays within
  $\tau$ on \extLocoPermInvGpt\% of permutations, against \extLocoNoiseInvGpt\% when the
  unchanged text is simply mined again (on ContraDoc this noise floor is exploratory, deviation D2). On ContraDoc, whose documents are nearly three times longer,
  the two shares are \extCdPermInvGpt\% and \extCdNoiseInvGpt\%. What moves the mined score is
  the miner's sampling, which grows with the number of claims, not the order of the text.
  gpt-oss-120b, sampled at temperature $0.7$, is noisier, and for it the order does matter
  somewhat beyond the noise: \extLocoPermInvOss\% within $\tau$ under permutation against
  \extLocoNoiseInvOss\% under re-mining on LoCoBench, and \extCdPermInvOss\% against
  \extCdNoiseInvOss\% on ContraDoc. What it extracts depends partly on the order in which it reads
  the text, a property of that miner rather than of the score.
\item \textbf{The baselines that win have no sampling noise.} They are deterministic functions
  of the text. DiscoScore RC and LC count repeated nouns regardless of order, so they never move on
  LoCoBench and rarely on ContraDoc, and the entity graph barely moves; with RC and LC excluded the
  comparison still fails, since the entity graph keeps \extLocoPermInvEntity\% and
  \extCdPermInvEntity\% of permutations within $\tau$ (App.~\ref{app:external}, D1). The G-Eval judge falls on \extLocoPermDecJudge\% of the LoCoBench permutations
  and \extCdPermDecJudge\% of the ContraDoc ones: it penalizes reordering as if it were
  incoherence.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Conflicts in natural documents.} Inserting a contradicting sentence into a ContraDoc
document lowers $\LCS$ with every claim true. It falls on \extCdAssertDecGpt{} of the
\extCdPairs{} pairs and rises on \extCdAssertIncGpt{} ($p<\extCdAssertPGpt$). In an exploratory
split, when the miner finds the contradiction, $\LCS$ falls on \extCdAssertEdgeDecGpt{} of those
\extCdAssertEdgeNGpt{} pairs; the remaining changes are sampling noise. The three-model admission committee of
\S\ref{sec-locobench} confirms that \extCdSpotContradicted{} of the \extCdPairs{} inserted sentences are contradicted by the rest
of their document. Read with that sentence false (exploratory), every relation the miner draws to
it is a support: \extCdEvSupGpt{} supports and \extCdEvConGpt{} conflicts, consistent with the sign
rule, under which a contradiction with a false claim is a support (gpt-oss-120b draws
\extCdEvSupOss{} supports and \extCdEvConOss{} conflict). The
document-level prediction H2a$'$ nonetheless failed, because the two versions of a document are
mined separately. Of the \extCdVerdEdgeNGpt{} pairs with a found contradiction, all
\extCdVerdFallsGpt{} whose score fell at the verdict world have no conflict on the inserted
sentence; they fell because other parts of their graphs came out
differently.

gpt-oss-120b finds the contradiction in only \extCdRecallOss\% of contradicted documents, so its
falls and rises are closer to even (\extCdAssertDecOss{} and \extCdAssertIncOss); where it does find
one, $\LCS$ falls on \extCdAssertEdgeDecOss{} of the \extCdAssertEdgeNOss{} pairs.

Recall is the bottleneck (Figure~\ref{fig:external}b). The miner finds \extCdRecallInsertGpt\%
of insertions but \extCdRecallReplaceGpt\% of replacements. It almost never finds a
contradiction that lies within a single sentence (\extCdRecallIntraGpt\%), since no relation
between two claims can represent it; this reverses the pre-registered ordering by distance. On
clean documents \extCdFpGpt\% of graphs contain a contradiction. The G-Eval judge falls on
\extCdJudgeDec{} of the \extCdPairs{} insertions and never rises, but the same judge also falls on
almost every permutation, so its falls do not separate a contradiction from a reordering.

\paragraph{The sign follows the truth on real LLM output.} On ChatProtect's self-contradictions,
every relation the miner finds between the two sentences has the sign the theory predicts at all
four assignments of their truth values (\extCpSweepNGpt{} cases). The miner finds the
contradiction in \extCpConfStrongGpt\% of the pairs annotated as contradictory and in
\extCpConfNoneGpt\% of the others. With every claim true, adding the contradicting sentence lowers
$\LCS$ on \extCpAssertDecGpt{} pairs and raises it on \extCpAssertIncGpt{} ($p<\extCpAssertPGpt$).
Where the contradiction was found (exploratory), it falls on \extCpFoundFallGpt{} pairs and rises
on \extCpFoundRiseGpt, so every rise is on a pair whose contradiction the miner missed. gpt-oss-120b finds
the contradiction in only \extCpConfStrongOss\% of contradictory pairs. Where it does, $\LCS$
falls on all \extCpFoundFallOss{}, but over all pairs its falls and rises are even
(\extCpAssertDecOss{} and \extCpAssertIncOss), so H3c fails for it.
On the pairs whose false side the annotators recorded, \extCpRealSupportGpt{} of the
contradictions found are supports at the real verdicts, because one or both sentences are false,
and \extCpRealConflictGpt{} are conflicts. Counting contradictions, as a consistency checker
would, charges all of them.

\paragraph{The miner against human annotation.} On GDTB, the senses that compile to no coupling
receive one in \extGdNoneGpt\% of cases (Figure~\ref{fig:external}c), against \extGdCorrectGpt\%
correct couplings for the senses that have one. Contrast and concession are almost never coupled
(\extGdContrastAnyGpt\% and \extGdConcessionAnyGpt\%); temporal sequences and unrelated adjacent
sentences are coupled more often (\extGdTemporalAnyGpt\% and \extGdEntRelNoRelAnyGpt\%). Explicit
relations are recovered better than implicit ones (\extGdExplicitGpt\% against
\extGdImplicitGpt\%). gpt-oss-120b shows the same pattern: \extGdNoneOss\% against
\extGdCorrectOss\%, and \extGdExplicitOss\% against \extGdImplicitOss\%. On QT30, pair-level F1 is \extQtPairFGpt{} (gpt-oss-120b: \extQtPairFOss):
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item inferences are recovered best (recall \extQtRecEntailmentGpt\%, direction right in
  \extQtDirGpt\%);
\item rephrases are often read as inferences;
\item conflicts are mostly missed (\extQtRecContradictionGpt\%).
\end{itemize}
QT30's annotators reconstruct implicit inferences between speakers, which our miners are
instructed not to emit.

\paragraph{What the checks show.} On data built and labelled by others, the score behaves as the
theory says:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item it ignores how a text is organized, beyond what the miner's own reading of the order changes;
\item it falls when a text contradicts itself and the contradiction is found;
\item each relation's sign follows the truth values in every case tested.
\end{itemize}
With GPT-6, four pre-registered predictions failed:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{H1a and H1c}, because the deterministic baselines barely move under
  permutation while the miner's sampling sets the score's own floor; they fail even with the
  order-free RC and LC excluded;
\item \textbf{H2a$'$}, because the two versions of a document are mined independently;
\item \textbf{H2b}, mostly through contradictions within one sentence, which pairwise relations
  cannot represent. That local contradictions are also found less often than global ones we did
  not predict.
\end{itemize}
With gpt-oss-120b the same four fail, and so does H3c: it finds so few contradictions that the
found cases, which all fall, cannot outweigh the noise in the rest. The binding
constraint is relation extraction, and on long documents the miner's sampling noise, not the
score.
